concept.title: Site search
concept.shortdesc: Search is powered by Pagefind, which indexes the generated pages after the build; readers get a fast client-side search with no server and no external services.

conbody.p: searchPagefindWhen search is enabled, every page carries a search field in the header — following the GOV.UK header pattern — leading to a search page, and only topic content is indexed — navigation, headers, and footers never appear in results. The index and the search interface are part of the output directory, so the site remains fully self-contained.

section.title: Enabling search
section.p: Search needs the Pagefind indexer on the machine that runs the build — and nowhere else. The plugin does not bundle it, and the published site carries the index and the search interface, so readers install nothing. Install Pagefind (a single self-contained binary; see its own documentation for your platform's installation methods), then build as normal: the default govuk.search=auto switches search on whenever the binary is found on the PATH, or at the location given by govuk.pagefind.cmd.

ul.li: auto — search on when Pagefind is found; otherwise the build completes without search and says so in the log
yes — search required; the build fails if Pagefind is missing
no — search off even when Pagefind is installed

section.note: Without JavaScript the search page explains that search is unavailable; everything else on the site works as normal.

section.title: Relevance: what ranks first
section.p: searchrelevancesearch-ignoresearch-demotePagefind scores like a general web search: a term's density counts, and long pages are penalised. In a reference publication that is backwards — the definition page for a term is long and mentions it constantly — so the plugin lets the DITA decide, and lets the publisher choose how results are scored.

govuk.search.ranking selects the scoring. default keeps Pagefind's behaviour. reference scores on raw term counts with no long-page penalty; measured on a 10,000-page data dictionary, it put the exact-title page first for seven of ten test queries where the default managed three. Any other need is met by passing a JSON object of Pagefind ranking options, for example {termFrequency:0,pageLength:0,metaWeights:{keywords:3}} (keys may be left unquoted, since command lines tend to strip quotes). A value that is not a preset or an object fails the build; an object that cannot be parsed is reported as an error and Pagefind's defaults apply.
The DITA itself carries the rest, translated into Pagefind's attributes:

ul.li: The shortdesc is weighted four times ordinary text: it is the most searched-for sentence on a reference page.

outputclass="search-ignore" on any element keeps it on the page but out of the index. Use it for cross-reference lists ("where used" tables, long link lists) that otherwise let a page that merely mentions a term outrank the page that defines it; in the measurements this was the only remedy for those cases.

outputclass="search-demote" on a topic or its title, or the topic's own importance="obsolete" or "deprecated", demotes the topic: its title weight drops to 2, its body to 0.3 and its short description to 1, so retired or superseded items rank below live items that share their words but remain findable. Weighting the body alone does almost nothing; the title weight is what decides.
Prolog keywords become searchable metadata, the natural home for "also known as" aliases; boost them with metaWeights.keywords in the ranking object.
A searchtitle becomes the result title, and prolog category and audience become filters, which the search page offers as facets when a publication defines them.

section.p: None of this changes how a page looks, and a publication that uses none of the markup is unaffected apart from the short-description weight.
